subject: chemistry-1
question: When solid sodium chloride dissolves in water, which interaction primarily stabilizes the separated sodium and chloride ions in solution?

options.text: Ion-dipole attractions between each ion and the oppositely charged end of nearby water molecules
Hydrogen bonds formed directly between sodium ions and the oxygen atoms of water molecules
London dispersion forces between the ions and the electron clouds of water molecules
New covalent bonds formed between the sodium ions and the oxygen atoms of water

explanation:
Water is polar, with partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charge on the hydrogens, so oxygen ends orient toward Na+ and hydrogen ends orient toward Cl-. These ion-dipole attractions are the strongest of the intermolecular interactions and build hydration shells whose released hydration energy roughly offsets the 787 kJ/mol lattice energy of NaCl. Because each formula unit releases two ions, dissolving 0.15 mol NaCl yields 0.3 mol of solute particles, which is why saline solutions conduct current and exert osmotic pressure roughly double that of an equimolar nonelectrolyte.

ELI-10: An ion carries a full charge and water carries partial charges, so the two line up: oxygen ends crowd around the sodium ion and hydrogen ends crowd around the chloride ion. Each ion ends up wrapped in a shell of oriented water molecules that keeps it separated from its former partner. This is not a hydrogen bond, because no hydrogen is being shared with a lone pair on N, O, or F, and it is not covalent, because no electrons are shared. Full charge meeting partial charge is called ion-dipole.
